title: The 15 things teachers need to know about learning
author: Martin Skelton
summary: This summary post in the Looking for Learning series gathers fifteen ideas Skelton believes anyone committed to learning needs, in the way a driver needs to know a few things about a car rather than everything about engines. It restates that learning should be the Hedgehog Concept of a school and requires a shared agreement about what learning is. The list separates learning from the factors that affect it, treats learning as a brain process, and stresses that sticky repeated experiences, not mere experiences, produce learning. It introduces the four states of learning (new, consolidating, treading water, drowning) and the idea of good struggle. It closes by distinguishing knowledge, skills and understanding as learned, taught and assessed differently. The post is a compact reference that sets up the definition of learning published the following week.
points: Only a small set of ideas about learning are essential for teachers, leaders and parents; the rest of brain research can be left to enthusiasts.
Curriculum, teaching, display and assessment are factors that affect learning, not learning itself, and confusing them is a persistent error.
Because the brain makes sticky whatever it repeatedly experiences, the quality and appropriateness of repeated experiences is a crucial lever.
Teachers need a simple framework for judging whether students are busy or busy learning, built on four states and the idea of good struggle.
Knowledge, skills and understanding differ in how they are learned, taught and assessed, and recognising this saves time and confusion.
quotes: It is the same for teachers who care about learning. Given the amount of brain research and popularisation that has been happening for the past 20 years or so, there are tons of things we could know about how our brains develop and work.

Learning is not a leadership thing. It’s an everybody thing. In my experience, most schools don’t have a shared agreement about learning, which makes conversations about learning and an ability to focus on it very difficult.
Curriculum, Teaching, Display, Assessment and so on aren’t learning; they are factors that affect learning. You can read more about this in the 12th February 2024 post.
Learning is a brain thing. Learning doesn’t happen in classrooms. It happens, everywhere, in brains.
The quality and quantity of repeated experiences is a crucial factor that affects learning. This is unbelievably important.
Experiences don’t equal learning. For something to be really learned, it must be hardwired and sticky over time.
Knowledge, Skills and Understanding are learned, taught and assessed differently. This is super important, too.
